title: Classes and Objects
summary: A class describes a kind of object. Each object can hold its own values and use actions defined by the class.
introduction: A class describes a kind of object. Each object can hold its own values and use actions defined by the class. Think of a blank book record that can be filled in for many books. Make two objects and check that each keeps its own facts.
learningObjectives: Define a class with __init__, instance attributes and methods that use self
Control how objects print and compare with __str__, __repr__ and __eq__
Distinguish class attributes from instance attributes
Reuse behaviour with inheritance and super(), and generate boilerplate with dataclasses

blocks.title: account.py
blocks.code:
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance

ada = BankAccount("Ada", 100)
bob = BankAccount("Bob")

ada.deposit(50)
bob.deposit(20)
print(ada.owner, ada.balance)
print(bob.owner, bob.balance)
print(ada.withdraw(30))
print(type(ada).__name__, isinstance(ada, BankAccount))

blocks.text: `class` defines a new type, and `BankAccount("Ada", 100)` creates an **instance** (an object) of it. Python immediately calls `__init__` on the new object to set it up, passing the object itself as the first parameter, conventionally named `self`. Every method receives `self` the same way, which is how `ada.deposit(50)` knows which account to change: it is really `BankAccount.deposit(ada, 50)`. Attributes attached to `self` belong to that one object, so Ada's and Bob's balances are independent.

blocks.title: Forgetting self
blocks.text: A method defined as `def deposit(amount):` fails at call time with `TypeError: BankAccount.deposit() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given`, because Python passes the object as the first argument whether you named it or not. Every instance method starts with `self`, and inside the method every attribute is read and written through `self.`; a bare `balance += amount` would create a local variable and leave the account untouched.

python point.py

blocks.text: Without these methods, `print(p)` shows something like `<__main__.Point object at 0x7f3a...>`. `__str__` is the friendly text that `print` and f-strings use; `__repr__` is the developer view shown in the REPL, inside lists and in debuggers, and ideally looks like the code that recreates the object. Define `__repr__` first: if `__str__` is missing, Python falls back to it. `__eq__` decides what `==` means, because by default two objects are equal only if they are the very same object. These double-underscore methods are called **dunder** methods, and there is one for nearly every operator and built-in.

blocks.title: class_attrs.py
blocks.code:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"     # shared by every Dog
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name             # unique to this dog
        Dog.count += 1

    def speak(self, sound="Woof"):
        return f"{self.name} says {sound}"

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")
print(rex.species, fido.species)
print(Dog.count)
print(rex.speak(), fido.speak("Grr"))
rex.species = "Wolf"                 # creates an instance attribute on rex only
print(rex.species, fido.species, Dog.species)

blocks.title: python class_attrs.py
blocks.content:
Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
2
Rex says Woof Fido says Grr
Wolf Canis familiaris Canis familiaris

blocks.text: Attributes assigned in the class body belong to the class and are shared; attributes assigned through `self` belong to one instance. Reading `rex.species` looks on the instance first, then on the class, which is why the class value shows through until `rex.species = ...` creates an instance attribute that shadows it. Use class attributes for constants and counters, never for mutable defaults such as a shared list, for the same reason as with [function defaults](/tutorials/python/functions).

blocks.title: inheritance.py
python inheritance.py
blocks.content:
I am Rex and I say Woof
I am Tom and I say Meow
I am Thing and I say ...
True False True

blocks.text: `class Dog(Animal)` makes `Dog` a **subclass** that inherits every method of `Animal` and may **override** some. `introduce()` is written once in `Animal`, yet it calls whichever `speak()` the actual object has; that late choice is what *polymorphism* means in practice. `super().__init__(name)` runs the parent's initialiser before `Cat` adds its own attribute, so the parent's set-up code is never duplicated. Keep hierarchies shallow: one or two levels is normal, five is a maintenance problem.

Many classes exist mainly to hold a few named fields. Writing `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for each of them by hand is tedious and error-prone, so the standard library generates them from type-annotated fields.

blocks.title: books.py
blocks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    year: int
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def age(self, current_year=2026):
        return current_year - self.year

dune = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965, ["sci-fi"])
emma = Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", 1815)
print(dune)
print(emma.tags, emma.age())
print(dune == Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965, ["sci-fi"]))
print(sorted([dune, emma], key=lambda book: book.year)[0].title)

blocks.title: python books.py
blocks.content:
Book(title='Dune', author='Frank Herbert', year=1965, tags=['sci-fi'])
[] 211
True
Emma

blocks.text: The `@dataclass` decorator generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the annotated fields, in the order they are declared. `field(default_factory=list)` gives each instance its *own* empty list, the same fix as for mutable default arguments. Dataclasses are ordinary classes: add methods, inherit from them, and pass `order=True` to get comparison operators for sorting.

blocks.title: Properties
blocks.text: A `@property` turns a method into a read-only attribute, so callers write `account.balance_in_euros` without parentheses, and a matching setter lets you validate assignments later without changing any caller. Reach for it when a value is derived from others or must be checked on assignment.

questions.question: `__init__` runs automatically each time you create an instance of a class.
questions.explanation: Calling the class, as in `BankAccount("Ada")`, creates the object and immediately runs `__init__` with it as `self`, which is where instance attributes are set.

questions.question: Inside `class Cat(Animal):`, what does `super().__init__(name)` do?
questions.explanation: `super()` refers to the parent class, so the call runs `Animal.__init__` for this cat, setting up the attributes the parent expects before `Cat` adds its own.
options: Runs the parent class's __init__ so Animal's set-up applies to this cat
Turns name into a class attribute shared by all cats
Deletes the attributes defined by the parent class
